issues.legal_issue: Adverse judicial remarks about a person who was not a party may be expunged when they were made without giving that person an opportunity to respond and are unsupported by the record or unnecessary to decide the case.
material_facts: The Chief Minister was not a party to the public interest litigation and was not asked to explain the file notations before the High Court made adverse remarks about him.
His role was limited to endorsing five applications with the routine notation “please put up”; the applications were then processed by CIDCO under its allotment procedures.
The High Court incorrectly attributed a further direction to him on another application, and the Supreme Court found no basis for the allegations that he had influenced the allotments.
issues.conclusion: The remarks and strictures against the Chief Minister were unwarranted and were expunged.
issues.legal_principle: Under the tests stated in State of U.P. v. Mohd. Naim and applied in Dr. Dilip Kumar Deka v. State of Assam, Jage Ram v. Hans Raj Midha, R.K. Lakshmanan v. A.K. Srinivasan and Niranjan Patnaik v. Sashibhusan Kar, a court considering expunction of disparaging remarks must consider whether the affected person had an opportunity to explain or defend himself, whether evidence supports the remarks, and whether commenting on the conduct was necessary to decide the case. Making serious adverse remarks without an opportunity to be heard violates natural justice. The Court also relied on A.K.K. Nambiar v. Union of India and distinguished the need for allegations to be properly supported when personal wrongdoing is alleged.

rule.if: expunction_appeal and affected_person_not_party and no_opportunity_to_respond and remarks_unsupported_or_unnecessary

predicates.expunction_appeal: An appeal seeks removal of adverse judicial remarks made about an individual.
predicates.affected_person_not_party: The individual criticised in the remarks was not a party to the proceeding in which they were made.
predicates.no_opportunity_to_respond: The individual was not given an opportunity to explain or defend himself before the remarks were made.
predicates.remarks_unsupported_or_unnecessary: The remarks lacked supporting evidence or were not necessary to decide the proceeding.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks removal of remarks about a non-party who had no chance to respond, and the remarks were unsupported or unnecessary, the remarks are removed.

issues.legal_issue: A state may maintain an appeal seeking expunction of judicial remarks when those remarks affect the functioning of a state office.
material_facts: The State appealed for the limited purpose of expunging remarks made about the Chief Minister, who had not himself appealed.
The State contended that the remarks affected the working and functioning of the Chief Minister’s office.
The Supreme Court accepted that the remarks reflected on the functioning of that office and held that the State could maintain the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The State was competent to maintain the appeal seeking expunction of the remarks.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the State could maintain the appeal because the remarks were capable of affecting the working and functioning of the Chief Minister’s office. The judgment cites no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this holding.

predicates.state_brought_expunction_appeal: A state brings an appeal seeking removal of judicial remarks concerning an office-holder.
predicates.remarks_affect_state_office_functioning: The remarks are capable of affecting the working or functioning of a state office.

issues.definition: When a state appeals to remove remarks that may affect the functioning of a state office, its appeal may be maintained.

issues.legal_issue: Adverse remarks about a public officer may be expunged when made behind his back without an opportunity to be heard and when they risk harming his reputation or career.
material_facts: The CIDCO managing director was not a party to the public interest litigation and was not given an opportunity to be heard before adverse remarks were made about him.
The High Court’s remarks accused him of serious wrongdoing and dereliction of duty and could adversely affect his career.
The Supreme Court found the remarks uncalled for and based on a misunderstanding of the facts.
issues.conclusion: The remarks against the managing director were expunged because they were made without hearing him and violated natural justice.
issues.legal_principle: An authority or court making comments that adversely affect a person’s reputation must provide that person an opportunity to be heard. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Lal Krishna Advani, which held that strictures should not be passed against an individual without making him a party and giving him an opportunity to be heard; Board of Trustees of the Port of Bombay v. Dilip Kumar Raghavendranath Natkarni, which recognises reputation as a facet of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution; and the natural-justice principles discussed earlier in the judgment.

rule.if: expunction_appeal and officer_not_party and no_opportunity_to_respond and remarks_risk_reputational_harm

predicates.expunction_appeal: An appeal seeks removal of adverse judicial remarks made about an individual.
predicates.officer_not_party: The public officer criticised in the remarks was not a party to the proceeding in which they were made.
predicates.no_opportunity_to_respond: The officer was not given an opportunity to explain or defend himself before the remarks were made.
predicates.remarks_risk_reputational_harm: The remarks are capable of harming the officer’s reputation or career.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks removal of remarks about a non-party officer who had no chance to respond and the remarks risk reputational harm, the remarks are removed.
